extraction.name: Visual Genome
extraction.description: Visual Genome is a dataset that connects language and vision using crowdsourced dense image annotations. It contains over 108,249 images where each image has an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects. The dataset includes seven main components: region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. Objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and question-answer pairs are canonicalized to WordNet synsets. The dataset contains 1.7 million question-answer pairs and is designed to enable modeling of relationships for cognitive tasks beyond perceptual recognition.
extraction.creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei
extraction.citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., Fei-Fei, L. (2016). Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. arXiv:1602.07332
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. Over 33,000 unique workers contributed to the dataset, which was collected over 6 months after 15 months of experimentation. Approximately 800,000 HITs were launched on AMT. The pipeline included collecting region descriptions, extracting objects with bounding boxes, adding attributes and relationships, building scene graphs, and collecting question-answer pairs. All data went through a verification stage using majority voting and rapid judgments.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Crowdsourcing (Manual Human Curator), Secondary Data analysis (images from YFCC100M and MS-COCO)
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: 108,249 images from the intersection of the YFCC100M and MS-COCO datasets. These are real-world, non-iconic images uploaded onto Flickr by users, ranging from 72 pixels to 1280 pixels wide, with an average width of 500 pixels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Data was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and QAs are canonicalized to WordNet synsets using Stanford NLP tools for noun phrase extraction and mapping to most frequent matching synset, with hand-crafted mapping rules for common failure cases. Region graphs are combined into scene graphs by merging co-referenced objects (bounding box overlap over union of 0.8).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Region descriptions were enforced to be diverse using BLEU score thresholds (0.7) compared against previously written descriptions. Bounding boxes required coverage (covering all objects in the description) and quality (tight around object, within 4 pixels). Attributes were normalized based on morphology (stemming). For relationships, prepositions were ignored and verb-synset pairs were mapped to WordNet sentence frames.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Workers were asked to: (1) draw 3 bounding boxes and write 3 descriptions per image, repeated until 50 region descriptions per image; (2) extract objects from descriptions and draw bounding boxes; (3) add attributes to objects and connect pairs with relationships from descriptions; (4) write question-answer pairs starting with one of seven Ws (what, where, when, who, why, how, which). Both freeform QAs (8 pairs per image with at least 3 different W types) and region-based QAs were collected. All annotations were verified via majority voting (3 workers) or rapid judgments for objects.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Verification was conducted using majority voting (at least 2 of 3 workers had to verify correctness) for most components, and rapid judgments for objects for faster verification. For canonicalization, workers verified mappings to WordNet synsets with 4 alternative options presented.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each image has on average 42 region descriptions, 21 objects, 16 attributes, 18 relationships, and 17 QA pairs. Verification involved 3 unique workers per annotation via majority voting.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique workers contributed. Geographic distribution: United States 93.02%, Philippines 1.29%, Kenya 1.13%, India 0.94%, Russia 0.50%, Canada 0.47%, Others 2.65%. Age range from 18 to 68 years, majority between 25 and 34 years old. Gender distribution: 54.15% male, 45.85% female. HITs achieved a 94.1% retention rate, with workers earning $6-$8 per hour.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford NLP tools (Stanford CoreNLP) including dependency parser for noun extraction; Stanford dependency parser for extracting compound nouns; word2vec for 300-dimensional vector representations; WordNet for canonicalization; VGG 16-layer CNN for feature extraction in baseline experiments.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains images of people (common objects are man, person, woman with 24K, 17K, 11K occurrences respectively). Images are somewhat biased towards people playing sports. Crowd worker demographics collected include age, gender, and geographic location.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, with 'ski', 'ballplayer' and 'racket' being the most common synsets. Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented due to image source bias. The dataset also has a bias toward certain common descriptions like colors ('white', 'red') and universal concepts like 'sky'. The geographic distribution of crowd workers is heavily skewed with 93.02% from the United States.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Canonicalization mappings are not perfect and contain some ambiguity. Relationships have high intra-class variability making prediction difficult. Answer evaluation works well for short answers but has problems when answers are long phrases. The questions have a long-tail distribution making trivial baseline models perform poorly on diverse question types especially 'where' and 'why' questions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training and benchmarking models for comprehensive scene understanding and reasoning tasks. Specific use cases include: dense image captioning, visual question answering, image understanding evaluation, relationship extraction, semantic image retrieval, attribute prediction, action recognition, and spatial orientation between objects. The dataset enables cognitive tasks beyond perceptual recognition such as reasoning about interactions and relationships between objects.
